verdict: Caution: lend selectively to Imphal handloom/handicraft units with verified festival and institutional order books and clean receivables; avoid leveraged single-channel weavers until cash-cycle data is collected.
title: Imphal Handicrafts & Carpets: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**Handloom and handicraft units in Imphal convert yarn and cane/bamboo into finished pieces sold through festive fairs, state emporia and NHDC channels.** The recent Mera Hou Chongba fair drew 42 stalls, with some recording sales over Rs 1.5 lakh across seven days [1][2] — that is the retail pulse, not a factory order book. Cash sits in finished-goods inventory and in festival receivables; value is in design and loom time, not machinery. **So when a proposal lands, check whether the unit sells through fairs/emporia or holds a repeat institutional buyer; if it is fair-only, ask for the last three fairs' stall sales.**

## Where cash and risk sit
**The cycle is short but lumpy: yarn purchase, weaving, then festive sale, so working capital peaks before each fair.** Rating methodology flags weaving as fixed- and working-capital intensive with high funding needs [8], and inventory management is a key rating sensitivity [9]. **So when a proposal lands, check inventory days and yarn stocking ahead of fairs; if stock exceeds one season's sales, ask for the ageing and the buyer list.** Capex is loom and workshop, modest, but term debt tenure drives coverage [10].

## What has changed now
**Local news is thin: the only Imphal datapoints are the October 2026 fair and a related seminar [1][2][3] — no city-level sales, order or credit data exists in the pack.** Manipur electricity demand is up 12.6% Apr-to-date versus India's 9.5% [D], a local activity tailwind, but that is power, not craft demand. Peer results are weak and dated: Golden Carpets' Q1FY27 revenue fell 53.6% YoY to Rs 12.05 lakh with a Rs 7.31 lakh net loss [5], and Priti International's revenue contracted 66.59% YoY with -3.78% operating margin [4]. **Treat peers as a warning on leveraged, single-channel craft exporters, not as Imphal evidence.**

## Where to grow, and how to grow safely
**Pursue weaver collectives and small units with repeat buyers — state emporia, NHDC, hotel and export buyers — and units adding a second channel beyond fairs.** Avoid highly leveraged single-fair sellers and pure trading intermediaries with no loom base. **Structure as cash-flow-backed working capital with a drawing limit tied to verified orders; take monthly stock and sales statements, quarterly buyer-wise receivables, and fair-wise stall sales.** For term loans, match tenure to loom life per rating guidance [10]. Collect from customer: yarn cost per unit, realisations, receivable days, and current lender exposure.

## Early-warning signs
**Watch for stock building faster than fair sales, receivables ageing past one season, and dependence on a single buyer or fair.** If stall sales fall below the Rs 1.5 lakh benchmark seen at the 2026 fair [1][2], ask for the next fair's bookings before renewing limits. If a unit cannot show buyer-wise receivables, treat it as unverified and hold enhancement.
watch: Stock exceeds one season's sales -> freeze drawing limit and inspect godown
Any single buyer above half of sales -> seek diversification plan before renewal
Sales below Rs 1.5 lakh per stall [1][2] -> ask for next fair bookings and cut limit
Yarn bought far exceeds woven output -> query diversion and stop fresh disbursal
